unit.title: CSS: classes, ids and links
unit.description: Linking a stylesheet, class and id selectors, inline styles, grouping selectors, which rule wins

cards.definition: A dot followed by a name, like .price: it targets every element whose class attribute holds that name.
cards.example: .price { color: green; } styles all the elements with class="price".

cards.definition: A hash followed by a name, like #header: it targets the one element whose id attribute matches.
cards.example: #logo { width: 120px; } sizes the single element with id="logo".

cards.definition: The HTML line, placed in <head>, that loads an external CSS file with rel="stylesheet" and href.
cards.example: <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> applies style.css to the page.

cards.definition: An HTML element, placed in <head>, whose CSS applies to that one page only.
cards.example: Handy for a quick test; a shared .css file is better for a whole site.

cards.definition: CSS written directly inside an HTML tag with the style attribute; it affects that one element only.
cards.example:
Sale

colors just this paragraph.

cards.definition: Several selectors separated by commas that share the same declarations.
cards.example: h1, h2, h3 { font-family: Georgia; } styles three heading levels at once.

cards.definition: When two rules with the same selector set the same property, the one written later in the CSS wins.
cards.example: p { color: red; } then p { color: blue; }: paragraphs end up blue.

exercises.prompt: How do you target the elements that have class="price"?
exercises.explain: A dot means class: .price targets every element whose class attribute contains price.
whyWrong: # targets an id, not a class.
Without the dot, the browser looks for a <price> tag, which does not exist.
This is not valid CSS: write just .price.

exercises.prompt: Which selector targets the element with id="menu"?
exercises.explain: A hash means id: #menu targets the one element with id="menu". An id must be unique on the page.
whyWrong: .menu targets a class, not an id.
menu alone would target a <menu> tag.
id:menu is not valid CSS.

exercises.prompt: The same class can be used on many elements of a page, but an id should be used only once.
exercises.explain: Classes are made to be reused: every product card can have class="card". An id names one unique element.
.promo only targets the elements whose class is promo. The second paragraph has no class, so it keeps the default color.
whyWrong: "New" has no class, so .promo does not touch it.
.promo only targets elements with class="promo".
"Sale" has class="promo", so the rule applies to it.

exercises.prompt: Which line, placed in <head>, loads the file style.css?
exercises.explain: The <link> tag, with rel="stylesheet" and an href giving the file name, loads an external stylesheet.
whyWrong: The <style> tag holds CSS directly; it has no src attribute.
HTML has no <css> tag.
<script> loads JavaScript, not CSS.

choices: Two: the h1 and the h2
exercises.explain: A comma groups selectors: h1, h2 { } applies the same declarations to both. h3 is not in the list.
whyWrong: The comma adds h2 to the list, so both are targeted.
h3 is not in the list, so it keeps its default color.
The comma is valid: it groups selectors.

exercises.explain: Same selector, same property: the rule written later wins. This is called source order.
whyWrong: The red rule comes first, so the blue one, written later, replaces it.
CSS never mixes two colors.
Both rules set a color, so the default black is replaced.

code.src:
p { color: red; }
p { color: blue; }

exercises.prompt: Build a rule that gives every element with the class "card" a white background.
exercises.explain: .card targets the class, background-color fills the box, white is the value.

exercises.prompt: The rule has no effect on <h1 class="title">. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explain: A class selector needs a dot: .title. Without it, the browser looks for a <title> element, which is not the heading.

exercises.prompt: Which way of adding CSS styles ONLY this one paragraph?
exercises.explain: The style attribute (inline style) applies to that one element only. Handy for a test, but hard to maintain: prefer classes.
whyWrong: A linked stylesheet can style every page that loads it.
This rule targets every paragraph of the page.
This rule targets every paragraph of every page that uses the file.
